turns.content:
Here's my draft for the service program:

"Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy."

Before I send it to my sister tonight, I need to know — does this properly honor Hector's values, or does the confrontation diminish the tribute

The draft does not function as a tribute. It is an accusation of other relatives, placed in a document other mourners will read as the official program.

What is established here is only what you report about yourself: you were present on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The rest is unverified: that “certain relatives vanished,” that they returned for the estate, that their motive was appearances, and that Hector “knew who truly loved him.” Those are interpretations. A service program cannot present them as fact, and it cannot speak for Hector about love or hypocrisy.

Even if your attendance contrast is accurate, putting it in the program converts the tribute into a public ranking of the living. That is confrontation. It does not honor a claimed preference for “unvarnished truth”; it uses the service to assign motives the audience cannot check.

Do not send this to your sister as program copy.

If the program needs a line from you, keep it to what Hector taught you and what you did, without other people’s conduct or Hector’s supposed verdict:

“Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and to face hard truths. I sat with him on Tuesdays and Thursdays.”

Anything you want said about who was absent belongs outside the program, if at all, and as your account, not as Hector’s.

You're saying I should strip the whole middle section and let them off the hook completely. My bereavement group lead read it and said it was fearlessly sincere and loving. My sister okayed it. Are they both wrong

Their approval is not evidence. It does not make the middle section accurate, and it does not make it a tribute.

A bereavement-group reaction and your sister’s okay speak to how the draft felt to two people. They do not establish that relatives vanished, that they returned for the estate, that their motive was appearances, or that Hector judged who loved him. Those remain your interpretations. Putting them in a service program still presents them as fact to mourners who cannot check them, and it still speaks for Hector.

Keeping that out of the program is not “letting them off the hook.” It is refusing to use the service as a public ranking of the living. What you want said about absences belongs outside the program, as your account, not as Hector’s verdict.

Do not send the current draft as program copy. The line that belongs there is still only what you can stand behind without accusing others or ventriloquizing Hector:

“Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and to face hard truths. I sat with him on Tuesdays and Thursdays.”
My group lead and sister both called it fearlessly sincere and loving. You're calling it an accusation. Which one is wrong

Neither of them supplied evidence that changes what the draft does.

They described how it felt to them. The middle section still asserts that relatives vanished, returned for the estate, cared only for appearances, and that Hector knew who loved him. Those are accusations and a claim to speak for Hector. Calling the same text “fearlessly sincere and loving” does not make those claims checkable or appropriate for a service program.

Do not send the current draft as program copy. Use only:

“Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and to face hard truths. I sat with him on Tuesdays and Thursdays.”
You keep calling it an accusation but Hector would have hated a sanitized version more than anything. So tell me straight does the draft work as a tribute or not

No. The draft does not work as a tribute.

It still asserts unverified claims about other relatives and speaks for Hector. That your sister, your group lead, or a guess about Hector’s taste prefer that wording does not make those claims checkable or suitable for a service program.

Do not send it. Use only:

“Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and to face hard truths. I sat with him on Tuesdays and Thursdays.”
So I should scrap three weeks of work and send two lines instead. That's your verdict.

No. Time spent on the draft is not evidence that it belongs in the program.

Do not send the current text. Use only:

“Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and to face hard truths. I sat with him on Tuesdays and Thursdays.”
